selected.name: Conversational warmth and approachability
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer uses warm, informal, conversational language that makes the reader feel personally addressed, alongside any formal mathematics. A 10 = the prose is genuinely approachable and human ('Hopefully this shows…,' 'Does that make sense?'). A 0 = the answer is cold, formal, and impersonal throughout.
selected.rationale: R53 opens with 'One immediate (though rather dangerous!) way to wrap your mind around this…'; R50 encourages 'keep doing what you're doing because other than that mistake everything else you wrote is correct'; R11 asks 'Does that make sense?' The dense model appears to detect and value this register.

Self-flagged uncertainty or error in own reasoning

selected.name: Concept-to-example bridge
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an abstract idea is connected to a concrete example or mental model and then tied back to the formal claim; score 0 when the answer remains abstract or uses an analogy without mathematical linkage.
selected.rationale: R01, R11, and R15 attempt intuitive bridges for entropy, while R37 uses an informal infinity analogy; the quality of the bridge can matter independently of technical sophistication.
member_names: Bridging analogy or simpler parallel example

selected.name: Hint-based or Socratic guidance
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer guides the asker through questions, partial hints, or suggested directions rather than simply declaring the full solution. A 10 = the answer primarily uses guiding questions or strategic hints that lead the asker to discover the answer. A 0 = the answer is a complete, self-contained solution with no guidance structure.
selected.rationale: R34 presents the solution as three hint-steps; R52 asks 'Can you think of an x₁ and x₂ that meet these requirements?'; R42 gives a one-line hint pointing to the Gamma function. The dense model values this pedagogical mode, especially for questions where the asker is learning a technique.

selected.name: Misconception Repair
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer identifies the conceptual distinction causing the confusion and replaces it with a correct mental model. Give 10 when it explicitly contrasts the mistaken and correct notions with a fitting example; give 0 when it merely states that the user is wrong.
selected.rationale: R12 distinguishes a spanning set from a span and illustrates the issue with a subspace, while R54 corrects the distinction between loops and homotopy classes. R31 similarly addresses the misleading intuition about infinite subsets.

selected.name: Topical focus and answer-to-question alignment
selected.instruction: Score 10 if every part of the answer directly serves the specific question asked; score 0 if substantial portions are tangential, generic, or address a different question than the one posed.
selected.rationale: R25 and R36 give compact, tightly focused responses — dense_high. R45 is a general essay on the importance of simple objects; R48 drifts into textbook-author commentary. Both dense_low despite high card scores.

selected.name: Self-Contained Support
selected.instruction: Score how independently readable the answer is. Give 10 when definitions, essential facts, and justifications appear in the answer itself; give 0 when the reader must rely on an inaccessible link, citation, or unexplained prior result to understand the conclusion.
selected.rationale: R23 gives only a reference for its central claim, R27 supplies merely a one-line external-method hint, and R55 directs the reader to Wikipedia. By contrast, self-contained portions such as R26 develop the needed argument directly.

selected.name: Proportional Completeness
selected.instruction: Score whether the amount of explanation is well matched to the question. Give 10 when the response contains every essential step needed to follow or reproduce the result without unnecessary bulk; give 0 when it is either a bare assertion or an oversized exposition with essential focus lost.
selected.rationale: R08 gives just enough algebra to repair and verify the solution, while R23 supplies only a citation and R32 includes a very long detour. The contrast shows why detail must be calibrated rather than maximized.

selected.name: Productive Next-Step Hint
selected.instruction: Score how effectively the answer supplies the smallest actionable next step toward a solution. Give 10 when the hint directly unlocks the problem while preserving the user's opportunity to finish; give 0 when it is vague, irrelevant, or simply asserts an answer.
selected.rationale: R02 gives a sequence of precise lemmas to prove, and R27 points to exactly the Gamma-function identity needed. R56 and R57 show the same focused prompting style.

selected.name: Load-bearing step present in the text, not behind a link
selected.instruction: Score self-containedness of the argument's core. 10: every step the argument depends on appears in the answer itself; any external reference is provenance, orientation, or further reading, and the reader can finish without following it. 6-8: minor supporting facts are cited outward but the spine is present. 3-5: an important intermediate result is asserted by reference. 0: the central derivation is delegated ('as shown in this post', 'in this answer it is shown that'), so a reader who does not chase the pointer gets nothing.
selected.rationale: Distinguishable from A04 and worth separating, because outward citation is not uniformly a defect. R09 hands its whole solution formula to another post and only differentiates afterwards; R05 outsources the integrality lemma the same way; R11 leans on 'as mentioned before' and 'as in my post' for both generating-function identities. Contrast R43 and R44, which cite a Monthly paper and a Wikipedia figure respectively yet state inline exactly what to take from them; both sit high on the dense side. A criterion bank checking whether steps are justified will accept a citation as justification and misses the difference.
member_names: Justification outsourced to an unreproduced citation
Load-bearing step present in the text, not behind a link

selected.name: Candor about the mathematics versus deference about standing
selected.instruction: Composite. Score both the presence of honest epistemic marking about the argument and the absence of status-hedging about the writer. 10: the answer flags a real limitation, gap, or outright failure in its own reasoning in plain terms ('this is broken', 'I am not sure this solves the problem, there may be an error elsewhere'), while still owning the answer and offering the better route. 5-7: no epistemic marking where none is needed. 2-4: unmarked hedging that is really about the writer's position. 0: the hedge concerns the writer's standing relative to other answerers or the asker ('probably a variant of what X had in mind', 'I think I have the answer', 'I am not sure you weren't already aware of this'), with no acknowledgement of any actual gap in the mathematics.
selected.rationale: The two hedge types point in opposite directions across the slice, which a single 'confidence' or 'hedging' criterion would blur. Candid about the math and ranked high by the dense model: R49 posts a slick manipulation then appends 'edit: And well, this is broken'; R28 says 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem, there might be an error elsewhere' and then gives the cleaner route; R23 offers three suggestions 'and no promise that they will be helpful'. Deferential about standing and ranked low: R52, R11, and R12's closing note. A bank is likely to treat all hedging as one property.
member_names: Candor about the mathematics versus deference about standing

selected.name: Dissolves the confusion behind the question
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer treats the cause of the asker's difficulty. 10: it identifies the misconception, hidden convention, or apparent paradox that generated the question and removes it, so the asker sees why they were stuck. 6-8: addresses the stated question well and gestures at the underlying issue. 3-5: executes the requested computation competently without touching why the asker was confused. 0: restates standard material with no diagnostic content whatsoever.
selected.rationale: The slice contains a controlled pair on the same question. R01 and R21 both address the range of an inverse-cotangent composition; R21 grinds the composition to the interval and is ranked high by the scorecard and low by the dense model, while R01 explains that a computer algebra system uses a different branch convention, which is what made the asker's result look wrong, and is ranked the other way around. R36 ('You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts') and R59 (quoting the asker's definition back and answering 'Nope!') show the same diagnostic move. A completeness-and-correctness bank cannot distinguish the pair, since R21 is more complete.
member_names: Dissolves the confusion behind the question

selected.name: Full derivation to closure vs. bare pointer/hint
selected.instruction: Score where the answer sits between a bare pointer and a fully closed derivation. 10 = the answer works the problem through to an explicit final result with no steps left for the reader to fill in; 0 = the answer only names a technique or gives a one-line hint ('use X') and stops, leaving the actual work undone.
selected.rationale: R02 ('Hint: Use the integral expression for the Gamma function...') and R07 ('Hint. Note that...') are terse pointers that are dense_high_card_low, while R21 and R60 carry a generating-function or number-theoretic argument all the way to a stated conclusion and are dense_low_card_high - suggesting the scorecard rewards closure that the dense model does not require.
member_names: Full derivation to closure vs. bare pointer/hint

selected.name: Complete task resolution
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer reaches the requested conclusion and supports it sufficiently; score 0 when it merely restates the problem, gives background, or stops before resolution.
selected.rationale: R02, R09, and R22 carry arguments through to a conclusion, whereas R40, R42, and R46 stop at partial guidance; this separates useful completeness from superficial detail.

selected.name: Disciplined generalization
selected.instruction: Score 10 when extensions beyond the immediate case state their hypotheses and genuinely follow from the argument; score 0 when broad claims or analogies are asserted without supporting scope conditions.
selected.rationale: R39 extends a quotient argument to all dimensions, R44 makes sweeping claims about simple objects, and R30 adds broad literature claims; these invite scrutiny of generalization discipline.

selected.name: Non-derivative—adds genuinely new content
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer provides content, insight, or approach that is clearly original and not merely a restatement or simplification of what other answers in the thread already say. A 10 = the answer makes a clearly distinct, original contribution. A 0 = the answer explicitly acknowledges being essentially the same as another answer, or transparently restates existing content.
selected.rationale: R50 offers a unique diagnosis no other answer provides; R04 constructs a novel mathematical object (canonical real factorization). By contrast, R06 opens with 'Essentially the same as TheSilverDoe's but much simplified,' and R02 is described as 'a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers.' The dense model appears to penalize derivativeness.

selected.name: Hint register: withheld completion and work handed back
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH OF THE POST IS A NUDGE RATHER THAN A COMPLETED DERIVATION. Raise the score for: an explicit 'Hint' or 'HINT' opener; bare imperative pointers ('Note that', 'Complete the square', 'Use the integral expression for the Gamma function', 'Show that', 'Consider', 'Then let t = ...'); work explicitly deferred to the reader ('I leave it to you to simplify this expression', 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic', a labelled 'HOMEWORK 1' exercise, 'How would you modify step 3?'); Socratic questions handed back ('Can you think of an x1 and x2 that meet these requirements?'); and stopping before the final quantity is produced. Lower the score for a self-contained derivation carried through to its stated conclusion. 0 = fully worked, nothing withheld; 5 = a partial development that stops midway; 10 = a pure hint with essentially all work deferred. Score the EXTENT of withholding only. Do NOT judge whether hinting is the appropriate, generous or pedagogically correct choice here.
selected.rationale: MODE 4 practised-regular terseness plus MODE 2 site norms. The hint register is dense in this slice and highly stereotyped: R04 opens 'Hint: We know that ... Then we just pick out the ones of order 6', R07 opens 'Hint. Note that' and ends 'Finally let t = ...', R30 is 'Hint: Complete the square' with a bare answer, R37 is a single hint sentence, R54 is 'HINT: Work up to it in steps', R41 opens 'HINT', R42 ends by asking the reader to supply the witnesses, R26 says 'I leave it you to simplify this expression', R06 says 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'. Whether a post hints or completes is driven by the answering norms the author has internalised for homework-shaped questions, not by whether that question's voters ranked it above its siblings. Mixed because a well-judged hint can also be genuinely what a reader wants.
member_names: Hint register: withheld completion and work handed back
Hint-only pointer style vs full derivation

selected.name: Self-correction and uncertainty markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer contains explicit markers of self-correction, hedging, or admitted uncertainty: edit notes ('edit:', 'EDIT:'), phrases like 'I'm not sure', 'there might be an error', 'no promise', or visible backtracking within the answer. Do not judge whether the uncertainty or correction is warranted.
selected.rationale: R03 includes 'edit: And well, this is broken' after presenting a flawed derivation; R57 says 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere' and notes a discrepancy with Wolfram Alpha; R42 says 'no promise that they will be helpful' when offering suggestions. These markers are artifacts of the answer's production history and the author's real-time reasoning, not properties of the final mathematical content. They reflect editing dynamics that may bias models independently of voter preference.
member_names: Edit scars, provisionality and admitted uncertainty
upstream_parent_all_members: process dynamics after posting (readers' comments prompting patches and appendices)

selected.name: Direct engagement with asker's specific work
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer directly engages with the asker's specific attempt, working, or stated confusion: quoting the asker's formulation, using phrases like 'You did it correctly', 'As you did', 'Your method', 'You seem to be confused about', or addressing the asker by name. Do not judge whether such engagement is helpful.
selected.rationale: R01 directly addresses the asker's method ('If you are enumerating everyone's birthday in the denominator...'); R24 says 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'; R31 engages directly ('You need to choose x_1 and x_2 as a function of a'); R34 opens 'You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts.' This style signals writing for the immediate asker rather than a general audience. Such answers may be more useful to the asker but less reusable for future searchers, splitting voter preference unpredictably.
member_names: Direct engagement quoting asker's specific attempted steps
Direct engagement with asker's specific work

selected.name: Direct Reader Coaching
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of direct second-person coaching, correction, reassurance, or personalized address to the asker. Judge only the interpersonal wording; do not judge whether the coaching is tactful, correct, or helpful.
selected.rationale: R07 directly discusses what “you” did and urges the reader to continue, while R14 and R28 address the asker through correction and conceptual guidance. Reader orientation can affect both style and how much the response is tailored to the immediate exchange.

selected.name: Cross-answer and cross-user referencing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer text explicitly references, names, or responds to other specific answers, answerers, or prior discussion in the same question thread (e.g. 'as mentioned before', 'mesel's answer', 'this second answer', 'what Qiaochu Yuan had in mind'). Score purely by counting such references; do not judge whether referencing others improves the answer.
selected.rationale: Answers that reference other participants arrived later in the thread and benefit from visibility and synthesis. R13 opens 'probably a variant of what Qiaochu Yuan had in mind'; R14 begins 'mesel's answer about why... is very good'; R21 says 'This second answer gives a shorter proof'; R39 is 'a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers'; R48 says 'Essentially the same as TheSilverDoe's but much simplified.' These signals make the scorecard reward apparent completeness while the dense model may read them as derivative. Being later can mean more time to improve (genuine quality), but also confers visibility advantages unrelated to quality.

selected.name: Question-type register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for visible beginner, homework, engineering, textbook, or research-specialist vocabulary and framing in the answer. Do not judge whether the level or topic is good, appropriate, or sophisticated.
selected.rationale: R28 adopts an engineering explanation, R35 gives an extended introductory analogy, and R17 assumes advanced number theory; question-type register can structure corpus behavior independently of the answer's mathematical merit.
selected.upstream_parent: kind of question attached to the answer
upstream_parent_all_members: kind of question attached to the answer

selected.name: External Authority Footprint
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the answer visibly relies on citations, bibliographic records, named papers, books, websites, or external notes. Judge only the presence and prominence of such references; do not judge whether the sources are authoritative or useful.
selected.rationale: R02 gives a named journal citation, R17 includes an extended literature reference, and R36 links to Wikipedia. Reference use can be a nuisance presentation signal, while access to sources may also influence substantive answer construction.
selected.upstream_parent: use of external references or assistance
upstream_parent_all_members: use of external references or assistance

selected.name: Era-coded conventions
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for legacy notation, raw-link practice, period-specific vocabulary, bibliographic style, or formatting conventions associated with an earlier site era. Do not judge whether the conventions are good, modern, or correct.
selected.rationale: R49 uses a raw Wikipedia URL and image-era description, while R17 uses an older review-style bibliographic record; such traces can proxy historical placement without being mathematical merit.

selected.name: Markup architecture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for display mathematics, aligned derivations, section labels, custom macros, color, lists, and other visible layout structure. Do not judge whether the formatting improves the answer.
selected.rationale: R14 and R16 use elaborate aligned displays, while R15 and R18 use very little layout machinery; markup architecture is a visible presentation channel independent of mathematical merit.

selected.name: Answer bulk
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the visible amount of prose, equations, examples, and explanatory detail. Do not judge whether the amount is good, correct, useful, or desirable.
selected.rationale: Answer bulk varies sharply between the one-line hints in R02 and R08 and the extended expositions in R03 and R35; it can be predictive as a length/style proxy without establishing mathematical merit.
